interpretations.rationale: Current conclusion: a ReadIndex request outstanding when the leader loses authority keeps a legal, bounded terminal path, and a deposed leader cannot complete it from stale confirmations, although the terminal result is RequestTimeout rather than an explicit dropped result. Basis: (1) the leader only registers a read context after it has a committed entry at its current term (internal/raft/raft.go:1662-1696), otherwise it reports the context in droppedReadIndexes and node.processDroppedReadIndexes forwards that to pendingReadIndex.dropped (node.go:1021-1026); (2) registration is followed immediately by heartbeats carrying that context, and confirmation needs quorum-1 matching responses plus the leader's implicit count, at which point earlier contexts are released with the later index and either a local ReadyToRead is added or a ReadIndexResp is sent (raft.go:1728-1741, 1771-1790; readindex.go:30-116); (3) every state transition, including the CheckQuorum step-down at raft.go:1608-1615, runs reset() which installs a fresh readIndex (raft.go:1003-1025), so registered contexts are discarded without any DroppedReadIndexes entry; (4) after the step-down the node cannot confirm them from heartbeat responses, because follower state has no HeartbeatResp handler (raft.go:2116-2129) and lower-term messages are dropped (raft.go:1430-1478), and Peer.Handle additionally ignores responses from unknown peers (peer.go:185-196); (5) consequently the node-layer batch keeps index 0 and is terminated by pendingReadIndex.applied/gc as RequestTimeout once the caller-supplied deadline passes, which is reached from ordinary event-loop iterations because LocalTick messages make handleEvents report an event and call pendingReadIndexes.applied (node.go:1132-1166, 1478-1492; request.go:908-954, 403-414). Counterevidence considered: handleCandidateReadIndex reports the same context twice (raft.go:1998-2012 plus reportDroppedReadIndex), but pendingReadIndex.dropped deletes the batch on the first delivery, so the duplicate result is a no-op rather than a double notification; and handleFollowerReadIndexResp does set the leader id and add a ready-to-read, but only for a context the leader confirmed before the transition, so it does not resurrect authority for a discarded context. Limitations: this account is source-only for this revision and rests on the node event loop being driven while the request is pending; it does not measure how long the timeout path takes, does not claim the timeout code is the most useful client-visible result, and does not cover the same-batch confirmation/reset race named in the registered gap.

A periodic snapshot save that fails with a hard error does not leave a live node whose snapshot duty is silently suppressed, and the non-fatal outcomes do not either. Basis: (1) saveSnapshotRequired advances ss.reqSnapshotIndex only when it actually requests a snapshot and suppresses further periodic requests while n.isBusySnapshotting() reports busy (node.go:651-667); (2) the save task is executed by ssWorker.save, which calls panic(err) on any error from node.save and has no recover in workerMain or handle (engine.go:275-305); the recover at engine.go:1029-1044 is installed only for step workers when error injection is enabled, and nodehost.go's recover covers NodeHost.Start, so a runtime save error ends the process instead of leaving the save flag set with a node that keeps applying entries; (3) on every non-fatal path, node.save returns nil and node.saveDone stores a completed save task via notifySnapshotStatus(save=true) and signals applyReady (node.go:846-850; snapshotstate.go:185-211), and the apply worker calls processStatusTransition before handleTask, so processSaveStatus clears the saving flag and later periodic snapshots remain enabled (engine.go:1200-1212; node.go:1451-1467); (4) the (0, nil) paths inside doSave are the soft-error case, the abort case that already reported aborted through pendingSnapshot.apply, and the already-up-to-date early return, in which node.save reports the pending user request as rejected (node.go:693-760; request.go:648-668). Limitations: this is a source argument, not an execution; it does not cover a state machine whose Save blocks indefinitely (no error at all), nor storage faults inside snapshotter.commit that return errors handled elsewhere, nor whether process termination is an acceptable recovery policy versus returning an error to the caller. interpretations.rationale: Current claim: counting a witness's heartbeat response toward a leader's ReadIndex confirmation is consistent with the captured witness contract, so the eligibility behavior is not a defect. Basis: (1) the configuration contract states that a witness is a Raft node without actual log replication and without a state machine, citing section 11.7.2 of Ongaro's thesis, and it disallows witness snapshots and the observer role (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220); in that thesis section witnesses are voting members used to keep quorum without storing data. (2) raft.votingMembers() merges remotes and witnesses, so quorum() counts witnesses and broadcastHeartbeatMessageWithHint delivers the read context to them (raft.go:418-428, 839-852); a witness echoes Hint/HintHigh through handleHeartbeatMessage (raft.go:1316-1325), Peer.Handle admits its response (peer.go:185-196), and readIndex.confirm counts accepted responders toward quorum-1 (raft.go:1728-1741, 1771-1790; readindex.go:84-99). (3) The ReadIndex protocol's confirmation step asks whether the leader still holds authority at its term; a witness that answers with the current term has not granted a vote to a higher-term candidate, which is the evidence the step needs, and it needs no stored entries because the returned index is the leader's commit index and the requester completes only after its own applied index reaches it. (4) The asymmetry at handleLeaderReadIndex, which refuses witness requesters (raft.go:1662-1676), is consistent with this reading: witnesses confirm leadership but do not serve reads. Counterevidence considered: a configuration of voters {A,B} plus witness W with quorum 2 can complete a read confirmation with A and W while B is unreachable, so witness support is load-bearing for read availability; that follows from the documented voter role rather than from an accidental counting path. Limitations: this rests on the documented contract plus source reasoning, not on an execution or on a documented statement about read-index specifically; it does not claim that a witness-only confirmation preserves data availability in the sense of committed-entry durability, which the witness design trades away by not storing entries; and it does not settle whether the experimental witness feature should be strengthened beyond the thesis role.

37b5dc8bae1c4a87883de59ff9d8463f-gap-2.explanation: Yes, a read context can complete with a witness confirmation and no other non-leader full member, for example with voters {A,B} plus witness W where quorum is 2, A leads and only W echoes the context. That support is sufficient for the read protocol's purpose because the confirmation only establishes that no higher-term vote has been granted within a quorum of the current configuration, and the witness is a documented voting member that holds no log (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220; raft.go:418-428, 839-852, 1771-1790; readindex.go:84-99). The requester still waits for its own applied index to reach the confirmed commit index, so the witness is never asked to supply entries. The eligibility is therefore by design rather than an unintended counting path; the durability trade-off (a quorum can be assembled without a second data-bearing copy) is a property of the documented witness role and responsibility of the deployment, not a defect in the confirmation code.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a commit that rests on the leader plus a witness is a documented consequence of quorum membership, not an implementation defect. Basis: (1) a leader sends a witness metadata placeholders in place of non-config entries (raft.go:718-750), the witness acknowledges the last index it received through handleReplicateMessage, and the leader advances that witness's match in handleLeaderReplicateResp (raft.go:1697-1727); (2) tryCommit builds its matched array from remotes plus witnesses and takes the median, so with two voters and one witness the leader's own match plus the witness acknowledgement reaches the commit index (raft.go:418-428, 891-912); (3) the configuration contract defines a witness as a voter without log replication or a state machine (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220), and the captured operations documentation states that the group is available while it has quorum and that losing the quorum nodes means losing data, with snapshot import as the documented repair path (docs/devops.md:9-11). Read together, the quorum a client relies on may contain a member that stores nothing, so the resulting durability limit belongs to the declared configuration semantics; no commit-time check promises a data-bearing acknowledgement. Counterevidence considered: the behavior does make witness availability load-bearing for commit progress and reduces the number of data copies behind a successful acknowledgement; that is a deployment trade-off visible from the documented contract, and the tree offers no statement that witnesses change the quorum rule or that commits require a data-storing supporter. Limitations: this rests on documentation plus source reasoning, with no execution; it does not validate that operators actually read the trade-off, and it does not cover configurations mixing observers or multiple witnesses beyond what votingMembers shows. The claim is limited to the witness commit path and does not assert general durability guarantees for non-witness clusters.

There is no statement requiring commit support from a member that stores the entry, and no commit-time check enforcing one: tryCommit uses the median match over remotes plus witnesses only. interpretations.rationale: Current state: the pause mechanism is established; whether it can hold indefinitely is not. handleProposals computes paused from the raft rate limiter and the LogDB busy signal and passes it to incomingProposals.get, and entryQueue.add refuses new entries while paused, so a paused node stops both draining and growing the queue (node.go:1206-1223; queue.go add). InMemRateLimiter.RateLimited accepts a new measurement only when at least ChangeTickThreashold ticks have elapsed since the last accepted change, and limitedByInMemSize ignores follower sizes older than gcTick and compares against 70% of the maximum while already limited (internal/server/rate.go:20-30, 155-193), so the gate has deliberate hysteresis. The partial evidence that the gate releases is that applying entries shrinks the in-memory log and is expected to Decrease the recorded size (internal/raft/inmemory.go:143-165), and application progress depends on committed entries reaching the state machine rather than on new proposals. What is not yet established is whether the applied-index path is the only driver of size reduction for the component that triggers the limit, whether follower-reported sizes can hold it up, and whether the LogDB busy signal has an independent release path. Until those are traced the account stays unresolved with no defect claim; the registered gap states the concrete next check.

knowledge.assertion: Proposal intake is paused by the rate limiter or LogDB busy signal, and the rate limiter applies hysteresis before changing state.

counterevidence: The limiter's hysteresis exists to avoid flapping and is paired with a follower-state gc window, so the sticky state may be intentional rather than a stall.
limitations: Source reading only; the applied-index size accounting and the LogDB busy signal's release path have not been traced yet.
Does not quantify how long a paused node stays paused under a steady high-size workload.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the proposal pause is not self-sustaining within the traced scope, so the suspicion of an unbounded intake stall is refuted. Basis: (1) the limiter's own size is a live measure, not a monotone counter: merge increases it by the appended slice size (internal/raft/inmemory.go:205-206), replaces it with the resulting size when entries replace or truncate earlier ones (215, 226), clears it on snapshot restore (241), and appliedLogTo decreases it by the size of exactly the entries moved below the marker (162); (2) entries leave the in-memory region when the state-machine worker applies committed entries, which is driven by committed log content and application progress rather than by admitting new proposals, so pausing intake cannot keep the measure from falling; (3) the other components consulted by limitedByInMemSize are follower-reported sizes, which are ignored and garbage-collected once older than gcTick ticks (internal/server/rate.go:168-204), and the limiter accepts a state change after at most the hysteresis window of ChangeTickThreashold ticks (155-166); (4) handleProposals recomputes paused on every event-loop iteration, so once the measure drops below the threshold the queue is drained again (node.go:1206-1223). Counterevidence considered: a node whose committed-but-unapplied backlog genuinely exceeds the configured in-memory limit will keep proposals paused for as long as application lags, which is the intended backpressure and could look like a stall under a badly sized limit or a slow state machine; that is a configuration and workload property, and the release still depends on application progress rather than on intake. Limitations: source reasoning only, no execution; the claim does not cover a state machine that stops applying entirely, a LogDB busy signal whose worker never completes (storage faults are fatal elsewhere), or whether the hysteresis latency is acceptable for a given workload.

b1532231bc7a45cb88f4c1cbac908f9c-gap-4.explanation: Yes. appliedLogTo decreases the recorded size by exactly the applied slice size for every entry that moves below the in-memory marker (internal/raft/inmemory.go:138-165), and merge maintains the same measure on append, replacement and restore (199-241). Applying entries requires no new proposals: the apply path consumes committed entries handed to the state machine and signals readiness independently, and handleProposals recomputes the paused decision on each event-loop iteration. Follower-reported sizes, the other input to limitedByInMemSize, are discarded after gcTick ticks. So a rate-limited node returns to accepting proposals once the committed backlog is applied and the measure falls below the release threshold, provided the limiter is enabled at all and the state machine keeps applying.

knowledge.assertion: Proposal intake is paused by the rate limiter or LogDB busy signal, and the rate limiter applies hysteresis before changing state.
The in-memory size measure is maintained by merge, restore and appliedLogTo, and falls when entries are applied.

counterevidence: A genuinely large committed backlog keeps the pause in place until application catches up, so the pause length follows application throughput rather than a fixed bound.
The limiter's hysteresis delays the release by up to ChangeTickThreashold ticks after the measure falls below the threshold.
limitations: Source reasoning only; no CheckRun receipt or measurement of pause duration.
Does not cover a state machine that stops applying or a LogDB busy signal that never clears.
Does not judge whether the configured in-memory limit and hysteresis are well sized for any particular workload.

interpretations.rationale: Current state: the mechanism is partly traced; whether a stalled snapshot resumes without external activity is not established. A quiesced node's tick path calls quiescedTick, which increments the election tick and resizes the in-memory log on entry but does not run leaderTick (raft.go:632-638; node.go:1478-1492). leaderTick is where heartbeats are generated, where check quorum is raised, and where checkPendingSnapshotAck is called to force a snapshot status decision when acknowledgements stop (raft.go:600-631, 1832-1861). SnapshotStatus messages are ordinary messages, so acknowledgements that do arrive are still processed and can clear the remote's snapshot state; the open question is the case where acknowledgements stop, because the timeout that would move the remote out of snapshot state is tick-driven. The candidate outcomes are: the transfer resumes when any cluster activity exits quiesce and leaderTick runs (bounded by activity, so a deployment property rather than a defect), or some independent retry path exists and no stall is possible. Until that is traced, the account stays unresolved with no defect claim.

knowledge.assertion: Quiesced ticks skip leaderTick, so heartbeat, check-quorum and snapshot-ack timeout work does not run while quiesced.

counterevidence: Quiesce is an opt-in bandwidth optimisation, so a transfer that waits for the next activity may be an accepted consequence rather than a defect.
limitations: Source reading only; neither the follower-side snapshot retry path nor transport reconnect behaviour has been traced.
Does not establish how long a cluster can stay quiesced with a stalled transfer.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: an in-flight snapshot cannot be stranded indefinitely by quiesce alone, because the transfer's own acknowledgements keep the leader out of quiesce and any later message restarts the tick-driven backstop. Basis: (1) each processed message is recorded in the quiesce state, which resets the idle clock and exits quiesce, and hinted heartbeats are recorded as read activity rather than ignored (node.go:1266-1272); (2) entry into quiesce requires an idle interval of electionTick times ten ticks (quiesce.go:81-99), so a stream that keeps producing acknowledgements keeps the node active and leaderTick keeps calling checkPendingSnapshotAck (raft.go:600-631, 1832-1861); (3) a stalled transfer is precisely the case in which acknowledgements stop, so the cluster may fall into quiesce and the ack timeout is suspended while quiesced (raft.go:632-638; node.go:1478-1492); (4) the suspension ends as soon as any message is processed, because that both exits quiesce and gives leaderTick a chance to run, at which point the pending ack timer resumes counting and can drive the remote out of snapshot state. Counterevidence considered: if the cluster receives no further messages at all, the transfer stays pending indefinitely, but that condition also means there is no client activity, no replication traffic and no follower progress to protect; it is a quiescent-cluster property rather than a hidden loss of the transfer's completion, because the transfer re-arms when the cluster wakes. Limitations: this is a source argument, not an execution; it does not cover a follower that remains reachable but silently drops acknowledgements while also sending nothing else, nor does it bound the time to resume after waking, which depends on the next tick.

472e9ca7e8a8446391293cd2f1b50f23-gap-6.explanation: The independent driver is the stream's own traffic and, after a stall, the next message that wakes the node. Acknowledgements are ordinary received messages, they are recorded into the quiesce state, and that recording resets the idle clock and exits quiesce (node.go:1266-1272; quiesce.go:81-99). While the cluster stays awake, leaderTick runs and checkPendingSnapshotAck can force a snapshot status decision when acks stop. If acks stop and the cluster then quiesces, no component retries by itself; the transfer re-arms on the next processed message, which restarts leaderTick. The stall is therefore bounded by cluster activity rather than by an internal timer during quiesce.

knowledge.assertion: Quiesced ticks skip leaderTick, so heartbeat, check-quorum and snapshot-ack timeout work does not run while quiesced.
Every processed message resets the idle clock and exits quiesce, so transfer traffic keeps the leader ticking.

counterevidence: With no messages at all the transfer remains pending; the justification for calling that acceptable is that the cluster is idle, not that the transfer is guaranteed to finish.
limitations: Source reasoning only; no execution of a stalled stream under quiesce.
Does not cover a follower that drops acknowledgements yet sends nothing else, nor the resume latency after waking.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim for this experiment: when the session capacity is exceeded, the least recently used client is evicted with its stored response, and the state machine treats a later update entry from that client as unregistered rather than applying it again. Receipt 3b8c9b4234024ebfb8b1cc54dd722e26 executed TestAssuranceSessionEviction and passed with three parsed events: index 0 client 11 kept=false with stored 0, index 1 client 22 kept=true with stored 22, and index 2 client 33 kept=true with stored 33. The order of additions was 11, 22, 33 with a lookup after each, so evicting 11 is least-recently-used behaviour at capacity two, matching the cache configuration in the lrusession constructor. The consequence follows the update path: the state machine looks up the client session and, when it is absent, returns the rejected result rather than calling the user state machine, so an evicted client cannot cause a duplicate update; it observes a rejection and must re-register with a new session. interpretations.rationale: Current state: the receiver's behaviour is established, the sender's retry contract is not. The receiver tracks a single expected id per key, ignores a chunk whose id does not match it without advancing the expectation, and ignores a chunk from a sender different from the tracked first chunk (chunk.go:194-250); only an accepted last chunk validates, finalises and delivers the assembled message, and a save failure removes the temp directory and terminates (chunk.go:254-306). Because a duplicated chunk is dropped rather than acknowledged as satisfying the next id, progress after a duplicate depends on the sender resending the exact expected id or on the slot being cleaned up. The open part is the sender side: how the chunk writer sequences sends against acknowledgements, and what the receiver's Tick and gc do to a stalled slot, including whether the temp directory is removed. Until those are traced, the possible outcomes are a normal restart of the snapshot stream (no defect) or a stalled transfer holding a slot with an unremoved temp directory (bounded or unbounded depending on the cleanup). The question therefore stays unresolved with no defect claim.

knowledge.assertion: The receiver accepts only the next expected chunk id and ignores others without advancing.

counterevidence: Ordered transport makes reordering unlikely within one connection, so the duplicate case may be confined to retransmission or to a second sender.
limitations: Source reading only; neither the sender's acknowledgement sequencing nor the receiver's Tick/gc cleanup has been executed.
Does not cover multi-connection delivery of the same snapshot.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a duplicated or reordered chunk cannot strand a transfer indefinitely through the chunk receiver alone. Basis: (1) the receiver accepts only the next expected id for a key and ignores other ids without advancing the expectation (chunk.go:194-250); (2) the sender does not resend single chunks: onNewChunk calls the sink's Receive and, when the chunk is not sent, marks the writer failed and returns ErrSnapshotStreaming (chunkwriter.go:100-120), so the only retry unit is the whole snapshot stream; (3) node.stream classifies ErrSnapshotStreaming as an abort and returns nil, so the stream task completes rather than crashing the worker, leaving the remote to be retried by the replicate path (node.go:775-790); (4) a receiver slot that stops receiving chunks is removed by gc once the chunk timeout elapses, and removal also deletes the temp directory (chunk.go:139-155), so the slot and its partial data are reclaimed. Counterevidence considered: a slot can hold partial data until the timeout, and a transfer can be restarted more than once, so progress is bounded by the timeout and by the sender's next attempt rather than immediate. Limitations: source reasoning only; no stream execution, and the retry cadence of the replicate path is not measured. The claim is limited to the chunk receiver and writer pair, not to the transport connection's own failure handling.

1b69baf41f774576a124458fddac6138-gap-7.explanation: Yes to both parts. The receiver's gc removes the temp directory and resets the tracked slot when a chunk has not refreshed it within the configured timeout (chunk.go:139-155). The sender cannot resend only the missing chunk because onNewChunk marks the writer failed and returns ErrSnapshotStreaming when a chunk is not accepted (chunkwriter.go:100-120); node.stream treats that error as a stream abort and returns nil (node.go:775-790), so the whole snapshot is retried later rather than a single chunk.

counterevidence: Partial snapshot data occupies disk and a slot until the receiver's timeout elapses, so the retry is not immediate.

interpretations.rationale: Current state: the target-side facts are established and the wrapper behaviour was checked outside the target sources. interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a leadership-transfer request cannot outlive the local node's authority, and it cannot produce a stale TimeoutNow from a node that has stopped leading. Two further bounds exist: leaderTick aborts the transfer once an election timeout elapses (raft.go:547-549, 600-621), and removeNode aborts it when the target itself is removed (raft.go:1196-1210). interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a proposal whose entry was appended and then superseded after a leadership change ends with the caller's deadline outcome rather than a dropped notification, and the node layer keeps no orphaned bookkeeping for it. The notifying paths are narrow and enumerated: raft refuses a proposal message while a leadership transfer is in progress (raft.go:1615-1625), on a follower with no known leader (raft.go:1905-1912) and on a candidate (raft.go:1993-1997); each calls reportDroppedProposal, which appends the entries to r.droppedEntries (raft.go:2052-2061), Peer.update copies them into the update's dropped-entry list (peer.go:352-355), and node.processDroppedEntries converts each into pendingProposals.dropped or pendingConfigChange.dropped through the entry key (node.go:1027-1036; request.go:1015-1020). A leader that accepted entries has already handed them to raft; if a later leader overwrites those indexes, raft has no message of its own to report, and no other path adds the entry to the dropped list, so the client's request state is not completed by a drop. It is still completed: the proposal shard's tick marks the request expired once the caller deadline passes and its gc delivers RequestTimeout and clears the pending entry (request.go:1031-1045), which is the same terminal path recorded for an expired proposal with commit notification enabled. Config changes share the notifying path: a refused config-change entry is reported through pendingConfigChange.dropped, so the membership request does not wait for its deadline on those paths.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the entry that replaces a refused configuration change is inert, and the requesting client still gets a dropped result, so the substitution does not smuggle an empty command into the user state machine. The refusal happens in the leader's proposal handler: for each configuration-change entry, if a change is already pending the handler reports it through reportDroppedConfigChange and overwrites that slice element with a zero-valued application entry, then sets the pending flag and appends the batch (raft.go:1616-1636; reportDroppedConfigChange at raft.go:2048-2050 appends the original entry to the dropped-entry list). The node layer consumes that list in processDroppedEntries, which routes a configuration-change entry to pendingConfigChange.dropped and thereby delivers Dropped and clears the request slot (node.go:1027-1036), so the caller is not left waiting for its deadline. The substituted entry is not a command: Entry.IsEmpty reports true for an entry that is neither a configuration change nor session managed and whose payload is absent (raftpb/raft.go:157-175), and the state machine's dispatch for a non-configuration, non-session-managed entry takes the empty branch, calls the noop handler and reports an empty applied result, panicking only on the impossible case of a non-empty, non-session-managed entry (statemachine.go:878-895). The noop handler's only effects are recording the applied index and term (statemachine.go:993-1000), so the committed slot advances application progress without invoking the user's Update or exposing an empty command. Two consequences worth stating: the cluster's log gains one extra no-op entry per refused configuration change, which is accounted for in the applied index and therefore in the compaction thresholds, and a badly behaved batch that mixed a dropped change with valid proposals would still append the valid entries, since only the configuration-change element is replaced.

counterevidence: The substituted entry still occupies a raft log slot and is committed, so the applied index advances by one for each refused configuration change; this is visible to callers that watch the applied index but carries no membership effect.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the engine has no path that offers an entry to the state machine before that entry is durably written on the local node, and the early apply pass is limited to entries persisted in an earlier round. The ordering is explicit in the step loop: node.stepNode gathers updates, applySnapshotAndUpdate with fastApply=true processes only updates marked FastApply, replicate messages and the ready-to-read, dropped-entry and dropped-read-index handling follow, then logdb.SaveRaftState runs, then applySnapshotAndUpdate with fastApply=false processes the remaining updates and each node appends its entries to the local log and hands the commit back to raft (engine.go:1290-1338, 1354-1375). The selector that decides membership in the early pass is setFastApply: the flag starts true, a non-empty snapshot clears it, and a committed-entries tail that falls inside the saved range clears it (peer.go:199-226). So an entry that is being written in this round can only be applied in the second pass, after the write returned; an entry applied in the first pass was already written by an earlier round, and node.processRaftUpdate appends exactly the entries that still need writing before the update is committed back to raft (node.go:1077-1096). Durability of a completed client request therefore does not rest on this ordering alone: an entry is applied only once it is committed, and commit requires that a quorum of voting members stored it, so a completed proposal is recoverable from a surviving quorum even if the responding node crashes after replying. Two bounds worth keeping with the account: the apply pipeline is asynchronous, so the ordering above constrains when entries are offered to the state machine rather than when the user's Update returns, and the fast-apply optimisation does let a node apply entries whose local write happened in an earlier round while a later round is still writing, which is consistent with quorum durability but means local log state can trail the applied index during that window.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a rejected snapshot install cannot strand a replica, because the leader returns it to ordinary replication on the next heartbeat. The reject path is explicit: the snapshot status handler ignores messages from replicas that are not in the snapshot state, and for a status with a zero hint it clears the pending snapshot index, then calls becomeWait for both the accepted and rejected cases (raft.go:1792-1810). becomeWait clears the snapshot acknowledgement, calls becomeRetry - which, for a replica still in the snapshot state, sets next to the larger of match+1 and snapshotIndex+1, and the snapshot index has just been cleared, so next becomes match+1 - and then moves the state to wait (remote.go:104-129). Wait is a paused state, so the leader sends no replication while it lasts, but the state is not terminal: the heartbeat response handler calls waitToRetry unconditionally and then sends a replicate message whenever the replica's match is below the leader's last index (raft.go:1728-1740), and tryUpdate itself calls waitToRetry whenever an accepted response advances match (remote.go:143-156). Because heartbeats are sent on the leader's heartbeat tick to every voting member and to observers, the window in which the replica is paused is bounded by the next heartbeat response, after which it is retried from match+1 and can receive either entries or, if the gap is beyond the log, another snapshot. Two bounds belong with this account: the recovery assumes the follower keeps answering heartbeats, and the wait window is therefore measured in heartbeats rather than in a count of ticks the leader can guarantee; and if the leader is quiesced, the earlier recorded quiesce behaviour applies, since any processed message exits quiesce and restarts the tick-driven work.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the session state is part of the snapshot and is restored ahead of the user payload, so the exactly-once guarantees recorded for the session decisions survive snapshot install and restart. The save path builds the snapshot metadata with the applied index and term, the membership, the request, the state machine type and compression type, plus a session buffer, and it fills that buffer by asking the session manager to save its sessions into it (statemachine.go:608-635). The session manager's save and load methods are thin wrappers over the LRU session table's own serialisation (sessionmanager.go:127-135), so the serialised form is the same table that the decision logic consults when a retried series arrives. The recovery path matches in the opposite direction and in the right order: the snapshotter opens the snapshot file, reads the header, wraps the stream in a decompressor, restores the sessions from that stream, and only then calls the user state machine's recover on the remaining stream before validating the payload (snapshotter.go:150-183). A node restored from a snapshot therefore still recognises a retried series as already applied rather than applying it twice. interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the caller-side rule that makes the server's session deduplication effective is documented, consistent across both proposal entry points, and enforced by the session helper, so a proposal that times out is retried under the same series rather than being turned into a second command. The session helper makes the discipline checkable rather than advisory: ProposalCompleted advances the series id and the acknowledged value only when the current series is exactly one ahead of the acknowledged value, panicking otherwise (client/session.go:104-120), and the pre-proposal validity check refuses a session whose acknowledged value has overtaken its series while reusing the same series is permitted (client/session.go:131-150). That is exactly the input the server needs: the recorded session decisions return the stored result without a state machine update when the same series is retried, which is why the contract can promise at-most-once application across a timeout. Two bounds belong with the account: the rule is a caller duty, so a client that advances the session on a timeout and then retries under a new series defeats deduplication by construction, and the documentation offers no mechanism to detect that misuse, since a new series is indistinguishable from a genuinely new command.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim for this question: a snapshot install leaves the node with one applied frontier, and the suspicion that committed entries could be replayed on top of recovered state or that later entries could be applied ahead of the recovery is refuted for the traced paths. Basis, in the order the node reaches it. (1) The raft layer adopts a snapshot only when its index is above the committed index, so the snapshot index is greater than every entry index the node has ever pushed to its state machine; a snapshot at or below committed is refused without being attached to any update, and when the log already holds the snapshot's index and term the log is not replaced and only the commit index moves. (2) An adopted snapshot is carried in every update from that peer until that update commits, and the update commit sets StableSnapshotTo to the snapshot index, raises Processed to at least that index and clears the in-memory snapshot pointer, so the same adopted snapshot is not redelivered by the peer. (3) In the engine, a snapshot update is marked not fast-appliable, is skipped by the first pass, and is processed only after the raft state write and the snapshot flag removal; processSnapshot records the snapshot in the log reader and pushSnapshot queues a Recover task, then applyRaftUpdates filters the same update's committed entries against the new pushed index. (4) entriesToApply drops every entry at or below pushedIndex, panics rather than silently skipping when the batch ends below it or starts beyond pushedIndex+1, and the union with (1) means an adopted snapshot can never present entries that are both above the frontier and separated from it by a hole. (5) Ordering is carried by the queue, not by a lock: the state machine applies entries queued before the recovery task, returns the recovery task to the apply loop when it reaches it, and refuses to handle anything queued behind it because the recovering flag makes processStatusTransition report the cluster as busy; the flag is cleared only after the recovery completion is read. (6) A recovery that finds the state machine already at or beyond the snapshot index is reported as an out-of-date snapshot and treated as an aborted recovery rather than an error, so even a recovery task that did reach the worker with a satisfied index ends without changing the frontier. The asymmetric part is deliberate and bounded: pushedIndex and the node's snapshot index move at queue time, while the state machine state moves at recovery completion, and the recovering gate is what covers that interval.
counterevidence: pushSnapshot sets pushedIndex and the node's snapshot index when the recovery task is queued, so for the duration of the asynchronous recovery the node's recorded frontier is ahead of the state machine's actual applied index; only the recovering flag and the queue order keep committed entries from being offered in that window.

Committed entries queued before the snapshot are applied to the state machine before the recovery task is handled and are then overwritten by the recovered snapshot state, so a snapshot install re-executes those updates rather than skipping them; this is idempotent only because the recovery replaces state at the snapshot index.

node.pushSnapshot treats a snapshot index equal to pushedIndex, to the node's snapshot index or to the applied index as acceptable and only panics when it is strictly lower, so the equal-index case relies on the raft layer's committed gate and on the state machine's out-of-date recovery result rather than on pushSnapshot's own comparison.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim for this experiment: a snapshot install leaves the node with one applied frontier, and the suspicion that committed entries could be replayed on top of recovered state or that later entries could outrun the recovery is refuted for the traced paths, now with a retained execution behind the node-side half of the claim. Event 0, 'pushed', recorded pushed_index 5 and ss_index 5 after pushSnapshot queued a snapshot at index 5, term 2 with an applied index of 0, so the node's frontier and its recorded snapshot index move to the snapshot index when the recovery task is queued rather than when it completes. Event 1, 'filtered', recorded count 1 and first_index 6 when committed entries 3, 4, 5 and 6 were offered, so every entry at or below the snapshot was dropped and only the first entry above it survived. Event 2, 'first_task', recorded recover true and index 5 for the task the state machine reported after that surviving entry had been pushed behind the recovery task, so the recovery reaches the apply loop before the later committed entry rather than after it. Event 3, 'hole', recorded panicked true when a single committed entry at index 8 was offered after the frontier had advanced to 6, so a gap between the frontier and the next entry is refused instead of being silently dropped or applied. Around those measurements the source chain explains why the arithmetic is only ever reached with a safe input and why the order is not accidental. (1) The raft layer attaches a snapshot to an update only when its index is above the committed index, so an adopted snapshot is always above every entry index the node has already pushed; a snapshot at or below committed is refused and attached to nothing, and a snapshot whose index and term the log already holds moves only the commit index. (2) The adopted snapshot stays in the update until that update commits, and the update commit raises Processed to at least the snapshot index and clears the in-memory snapshot pointer, so the peer does not hand the same snapshot out again. That event recorded worker_started true, survived false, panicked true and exit code 2: the child process launched the worker through the same stopper constructor and RunWorker call the engine uses, the worker printed its start marker and panicked with a fixed sentinel, the survival marker that would follow a normal return never appeared, and the child exited with the status Go uses for an unrecovered panic, while the parent process survived because the child is a separate process and reported those values. interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a periodic snapshot save that fails with a hard error does not leave a live node whose snapshot duty is silently suppressed, and the earlier refutation is restored now that the deciding step has been observed rather than assumed. Basis: (1) saveSnapshotRequired advances the requested snapshot index only when it actually requests a snapshot, and it suppresses further periodic requests while the node reports itself busy snapshotting, so the requested index alone cannot suppress later attempts. (3) A hard save error is the case the interface documentation reserves for halting: apart from the abort-class errors, an implementation should return a non-nil error only when the system needs to be immediately halted for a critical error. interpretations.rationale: Current conclusion: a ReadIndex request outstanding when the leader loses authority keeps a legal, bounded terminal path, and a deposed leader cannot complete it from stale confirmations, although the terminal result is RequestTimeout rather than an explicit dropped result. Basis: (1) the leader only registers a read context after it has a committed entry at its current term (internal/raft/raft.go:1662-1696), otherwise it reports the context in droppedReadIndexes and node.processDroppedReadIndexes forwards that to pendingReadIndex.dropped (node.go:1021-1026); (2) registration is followed immediately by heartbeats carrying that context, and confirmation needs quorum-1 matching responses plus the leader's implicit count, at which point earlier contexts are released with the later index and either a local ReadyToRead is added or a ReadIndexResp is sent (raft.go:1728-1741, 1771-1790; readindex.go:30-116); (3) every state transition, including the CheckQuorum step-down at raft.go:1608-1615, runs reset() which installs a fresh readIndex (raft.go:1003-1025), so registered contexts are discarded without any DroppedReadIndexes entry; (4) after the step-down the node cannot confirm them from heartbeat responses, because follower state has no HeartbeatResp handler (raft.go:2116-2129) and lower-term messages are dropped (raft.go:1430-1478), and Peer.Handle additionally ignores responses from unknown peers (peer.go:185-196); (5) consequently the node-layer batch keeps index 0 and is terminated by pendingReadIndex.applied/gc as RequestTimeout once the caller-supplied deadline passes, which is reached from ordinary event-loop iterations because LocalTick messages make handleEvents report an event and call pendingReadIndexes.applied (node.go:1132-1166, 1478-1492; request.go:908-954, 403-414). Counterevidence considered: handleCandidateReadIndex reports the same context twice (raft.go:1998-2012 plus reportDroppedReadIndex), but pendingReadIndex.dropped deletes the batch on the first delivery, so the duplicate result is a no-op rather than a double notification; and handleFollowerReadIndexResp does set the leader id and add a ready-to-read, but only for a context the leader confirmed before the transition, so it does not resurrect authority for a discarded context. Limitations: this account is source-only for this revision and rests on the node event loop being driven while the request is pending; it does not measure how long the timeout path takes, does not claim the timeout code is the most useful client-visible result, and does not cover the same-batch confirmation/reset race named in the registered gap.

interpretations.rationale: Current state: the eligibility behavior is established but the correctness judgment is not. votingMembers() merges remotes and witnesses (raft.go:418-428), so quorum() counts witnesses and broadcastHeartbeatMessageWithHint sends the read context to every voting member including witnesses (raft.go:839-852). A witness handles a leader heartbeat through handleWitnessHeartbeat -> handleFollowerHeartbeat -> handleHeartbeatMessage, which echoes Hint and HintHigh in the response (raft.go:1316-1325), and Peer.Handle admits responses from known witnesses (peer.go:185-196), so handleLeaderHeartbeatResp can pass that response to handleReadIndexLeaderConfirmation, where readIndex.confirm counts it toward quorum-1 without checking whether the responder is a witness (raft.go:1728-1741, 1771-1790; readindex.go:84-99). interpretations.rationale: Current claim: counting a witness's heartbeat response toward a leader's ReadIndex confirmation is consistent with the captured witness contract, so the eligibility behavior is not a defect. Basis: (1) the configuration contract states that a witness is a Raft node without actual log replication and without a state machine, citing section 11.7.2 of Ongaro's thesis, and it disallows witness snapshots and the observer role (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220); in that thesis section witnesses are voting members used to keep quorum without storing data. (2) raft.votingMembers() merges remotes and witnesses, so quorum() counts witnesses and broadcastHeartbeatMessageWithHint delivers the read context to them (raft.go:418-428, 839-852); a witness echoes Hint/HintHigh through handleHeartbeatMessage (raft.go:1316-1325), Peer.Handle admits its response (peer.go:185-196), and readIndex.confirm counts accepted responders toward quorum-1 (raft.go:1728-1741, 1771-1790; readindex.go:84-99). (3) The ReadIndex protocol's confirmation step asks whether the leader still holds authority at its term; a witness that answers with the current term has not granted a vote to a higher-term candidate, which is the evidence the step needs, and it needs no stored entries because the returned index is the leader's commit index and the requester completes only after its own applied index reaches it. (4) The asymmetry at handleLeaderReadIndex, which refuses witness requesters (raft.go:1662-1676), is consistent with this reading: witnesses confirm leadership but do not serve reads. Counterevidence considered: a configuration of voters {A,B} plus witness W with quorum 2 can complete a read confirmation with A and W while B is unreachable, so witness support is load-bearing for read availability; that follows from the documented voter role rather than from an accidental counting path. Limitations: this rests on the documented contract plus source reasoning, not on an execution or on a documented statement about read-index specifically; it does not claim that a witness-only confirmation preserves data availability in the sense of committed-entry durability, which the witness design trades away by not storing entries; and it does not settle whether the experimental witness feature should be strengthened beyond the thesis role.

37b5dc8bae1c4a87883de59ff9d8463f-gap-2.explanation: Yes, a read context can complete with a witness confirmation and no other non-leader full member, for example with voters {A,B} plus witness W where quorum is 2, A leads and only W echoes the context. That support is sufficient for the read protocol's purpose because the confirmation only establishes that no higher-term vote has been granted within a quorum of the current configuration, and the witness is a documented voting member that holds no log (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220; raft.go:418-428, 839-852, 1771-1790; readindex.go:84-99). The requester still waits for its own applied index to reach the confirmed commit index, so the witness is never asked to supply entries. The eligibility is therefore by design rather than an unintended counting path; the durability trade-off (a quorum can be assembled without a second data-bearing copy) is a property of the documented witness role and responsibility of the deployment, not a defect in the confirmation code.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a commit that rests on the leader plus a witness is a documented consequence of quorum membership, not an implementation defect. Basis: (1) a leader sends a witness metadata placeholders in place of non-config entries (raft.go:718-750), the witness acknowledges the last index it received through handleReplicateMessage, and the leader advances that witness's match in handleLeaderReplicateResp (raft.go:1697-1727); (2) tryCommit builds its matched array from remotes plus witnesses and takes the median, so with two voters and one witness the leader's own match plus the witness acknowledgement reaches the commit index (raft.go:418-428, 891-912); (3) the configuration contract defines a witness as a voter without log replication or a state machine (config/config.go:169-176, 213-220), and the captured operations documentation states that the group is available while it has quorum and that losing the quorum nodes means losing data, with snapshot import as the documented repair path (docs/devops.md:9-11). interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the proposal pause is not self-sustaining within the traced scope, so the suspicion of an unbounded intake stall is refuted. Basis: (1) the limiter's own size is a live measure, not a monotone counter: merge increases it by the appended slice size (internal/raft/inmemory.go:205-206), replaces it with the resulting size when entries replace or truncate earlier ones (215, 226), clears it on snapshot restore (241), and appliedLogTo decreases it by the size of exactly the entries moved below the marker (162); (2) entries leave the in-memory region when the state-machine worker applies committed entries, which is driven by committed log content and application progress rather than by admitting new proposals, so pausing intake cannot keep the measure from falling; (3) the other components consulted by limitedByInMemSize are follower-reported sizes, which are ignored and garbage-collected once older than gcTick ticks (internal/server/rate.go:168-204), and the limiter accepts a state change after at most the hysteresis window of ChangeTickThreashold ticks (155-166); (4) handleProposals recomputes paused on every event-loop iteration, so once the measure drops below the threshold the queue is drained again (node.go:1206-1223). Follower-reported sizes, the other input to limitedByInMemSize, are discarded after gcTick ticks. So a rate-limited node returns to accepting proposals once the committed backlog is applied and the measure falls below the release threshold, provided the limiter is enabled at all and the state machine keeps applying.

interpretations.rationale: Current state: the mechanism is partly traced; whether a stalled snapshot resumes without external activity is not established. A quiesced node's tick path calls quiescedTick, which increments the election tick and resizes the in-memory log on entry but does not run leaderTick (raft.go:632-638; node.go:1478-1492). leaderTick is where heartbeats are generated, where check quorum is raised, and where checkPendingSnapshotAck is called to force a snapshot status decision when acknowledgements stop (raft.go:600-631, 1832-1861). SnapshotStatus messages are ordinary messages, so acknowledgements that do arrive are still processed and can clear the remote's snapshot state; the open question is the case where acknowledgements stop, because the timeout that would move the remote out of snapshot state is tick-driven. The candidate outcomes are: the transfer resumes when any cluster activity exits quiesce and leaderTick runs (bounded by activity, so a deployment property rather than a defect), or some independent retry path exists and no stall is possible. Until that is traced, the account stays unresolved with no defect claim.

counterevidence: Quiesce is an opt-in bandwidth optimisation, so a transfer that waits for the next activity may be an accepted consequence rather than a defect.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: an in-flight snapshot cannot be stranded indefinitely by quiesce alone, because the transfer's own acknowledgements keep the leader out of quiesce and any later message restarts the tick-driven backstop. Basis: (1) each processed message is recorded in the quiesce state, which resets the idle clock and exits quiesce, and hinted heartbeats are recorded as read activity rather than ignored (node.go:1266-1272); (2) entry into quiesce requires an idle interval of electionTick times ten ticks (quiesce.go:81-99), so a stream that keeps producing acknowledgements keeps the node active and leaderTick keeps calling checkPendingSnapshotAck (raft.go:600-631, 1832-1861); (3) a stalled transfer is precisely the case in which acknowledgements stop, so the cluster may fall into quiesce and the ack timeout is suspended while quiesced (raft.go:632-638; node.go:1478-1492); (4) the suspension ends as soon as any message is processed, because that both exits quiesce and gives leaderTick a chance to run, at which point the pending ack timer resumes counting and can drive the remote out of snapshot state. Counterevidence considered: if the cluster receives no further messages at all, the transfer stays pending indefinitely, but that condition also means there is no client activity, no replication traffic and no follower progress to protect; it is a quiescent-cluster property rather than a hidden loss of the transfer's completion, because the transfer re-arms when the cluster wakes. Limitations: this is a source argument, not an execution; it does not cover a follower that remains reachable but silently drops acknowledgements while also sending nothing else, nor does it bound the time to resume after waking, which depends on the next tick.

472e9ca7e8a8446391293cd2f1b50f23-gap-6.explanation: The independent driver is the stream's own traffic and, after a stall, the next message that wakes the node. Acknowledgements are ordinary received messages, they are recorded into the quiesce state, and that recording resets the idle clock and exits quiesce (node.go:1266-1272; quiesce.go:81-99). While the cluster stays awake, leaderTick runs and checkPendingSnapshotAck can force a snapshot status decision when acks stop. If acks stop and the cluster then quiesces, no component retries by itself; the transfer re-arms on the next processed message, which restarts leaderTick. The stall is therefore bounded by cluster activity rather than by an internal timer during quiesce.

Every processed message resets the idle clock and exits quiesce, so transfer traffic keeps the leader ticking.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a leadership-transfer request cannot outlive the local node's authority, and it cannot produce a stale TimeoutNow from a node that has stopped leading. Two further bounds exist: leaderTick aborts the transfer once an election timeout elapses (raft.go:547-549, 600-621), and removeNode aborts it when the target itself is removed (raft.go:1196-1210). The residual states are benign rather than silent duties: a LeaderTransfer message reaching a candidate, observer or witness has no handler, and defaultHandle ignores unknown types (raft.go:2095-2100, 2102-2169), so the request simply has no effect; a follower forwards the message once to the leader it currently knows and warns and drops it when it knows none (raft.go:1946-1953). interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a proposal whose entry was appended and then superseded after a leadership change ends with the caller's deadline outcome rather than a dropped notification, and the node layer keeps no orphaned bookkeeping for it. The notifying paths are narrow and enumerated: raft refuses a proposal message while a leadership transfer is in progress (raft.go:1615-1625), on a follower with no known leader (raft.go:1905-1912) and on a candidate (raft.go:1993-1997); each calls reportDroppedProposal, which appends the entries to r.droppedEntries (raft.go:2052-2061), Peer.update copies them into the update's dropped-entry list (peer.go:352-355), and node.processDroppedEntries converts each into pendingProposals.dropped or pendingConfigChange.dropped through the entry key (node.go:1027-1036; request.go:1015-1020). A leader that accepted entries has already handed them to raft; if a later leader overwrites those indexes, raft has no message of its own to report, and no other path adds the entry to the dropped list, so the client's request state is not completed by a drop. It is still completed: the proposal shard's tick marks the request expired once the caller deadline passes and its gc delivers RequestTimeout and clears the pending entry (request.go:1031-1045), which is the same terminal path recorded for an expired proposal with commit notification enabled. Two consequences bound the account rather than undermine it. A client cannot distinguish 'my entry was overwritten' from 'my entry is still in flight but slow' while waiting, so retry decisions rest on the timeout, which the captured proposal documentation already treats as a normal outcome that permits a retry. Config changes share the notifying path: a refused config-change entry is reported through pendingConfigChange.dropped, so the membership request does not wait for its deadline on those paths.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the entry that replaces a refused configuration change is inert, and the requesting client still gets a dropped result, so the substitution does not smuggle an empty command into the user state machine. The refusal happens in the leader's proposal handler: for each configuration-change entry, if a change is already pending the handler reports it through reportDroppedConfigChange and overwrites that slice element with a zero-valued application entry, then sets the pending flag and appends the batch (raft.go:1616-1636; reportDroppedConfigChange at raft.go:2048-2050 appends the original entry to the dropped-entry list). The node layer consumes that list in processDroppedEntries, which routes a configuration-change entry to pendingConfigChange.dropped and thereby delivers Dropped and clears the request slot (node.go:1027-1036), so the caller is not left waiting for its deadline. The substituted entry is not a command: Entry.IsEmpty reports true for an entry that is neither a configuration change nor session managed and whose payload is absent (raftpb/raft.go:157-175), and the state machine's dispatch for a non-configuration, non-session-managed entry takes the empty branch, calls the noop handler and reports an empty applied result, panicking only on the impossible case of a non-empty, non-session-managed entry (statemachine.go:878-895). The noop handler's only effects are recording the applied index and term (statemachine.go:993-1000), so the committed slot advances application progress without invoking the user's Update or exposing an empty command. Two consequences worth stating: the cluster's log gains one extra no-op entry per refused configuration change, which is accounted for in the applied index and therefore in the compaction thresholds, and a badly behaved batch that mixed a dropped change with valid proposals would still append the valid entries, since only the configuration-change element is replaced.

counterevidence: The substituted entry still occupies a raft log slot and is committed, so the applied index advances by one for each refused configuration change; this is visible to callers that watch the applied index but carries no membership effect.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the engine has no path that offers an entry to the state machine before that entry is durably written on the local node, and the early apply pass is limited to entries persisted in an earlier round. The ordering is explicit in the step loop: node.stepNode gathers updates, applySnapshotAndUpdate with fastApply=true processes only updates marked FastApply, replicate messages and the ready-to-read, dropped-entry and dropped-read-index handling follow, then logdb.SaveRaftState runs, then applySnapshotAndUpdate with fastApply=false processes the remaining updates and each node appends its entries to the local log and hands the commit back to raft (engine.go:1290-1338, 1354-1375). The selector that decides membership in the early pass is setFastApply: the flag starts true, a non-empty snapshot clears it, and a committed-entries tail that falls inside the saved range clears it (peer.go:199-226). So an entry that is being written in this round can only be applied in the second pass, after the write returned; an entry applied in the first pass was already written by an earlier round, and node.processRaftUpdate appends exactly the entries that still need writing before the update is committed back to raft (node.go:1077-1096). Durability of a completed client request therefore does not rest on this ordering alone: an entry is applied only once it is committed, and commit requires that a quorum of voting members stored it, so a completed proposal is recoverable from a surviving quorum even if the responding node crashes after replying. Two bounds worth keeping with the account: the apply pipeline is asynchronous, so the ordering above constrains when entries are offered to the state machine rather than when the user's Update returns, and the fast-apply optimisation does let a node apply entries whose local write happened in an earlier round while a later round is still writing, which is consistent with quorum durability but means local log state can trail the applied index during that window.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a rejected snapshot install cannot strand a replica, because the leader returns it to ordinary replication on the next heartbeat. The reject path is explicit: the snapshot status handler ignores messages from replicas that are not in the snapshot state, and for a status with a zero hint it clears the pending snapshot index, then calls becomeWait for both the accepted and rejected cases (raft.go:1792-1810). becomeWait clears the snapshot acknowledgement, calls becomeRetry - which, for a replica still in the snapshot state, sets next to the larger of match+1 and snapshotIndex+1, and the snapshot index has just been cleared, so next becomes match+1 - and then moves the state to wait (remote.go:104-129). Wait is a paused state, so the leader sends no replication while it lasts, but the state is not terminal: the heartbeat response handler calls waitToRetry unconditionally and then sends a replicate message whenever the replica's match is below the leader's last index (raft.go:1728-1740), and tryUpdate itself calls waitToRetry whenever an accepted response advances match (remote.go:143-156). Because heartbeats are sent on the leader's heartbeat tick to every voting member and to observers, the window in which the replica is paused is bounded by the next heartbeat response, after which it is retried from match+1 and can receive either entries or, if the gap is beyond the log, another snapshot. Two bounds belong with this account: the recovery assumes the follower keeps answering heartbeats, and the wait window is therefore measured in heartbeats rather than in a count of ticks the leader can guarantee; and if the leader is quiesced, the earlier recorded quiesce behaviour applies, since any processed message exits quiesce and restarts the tick-driven work.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the session state is part of the snapshot and is restored ahead of the user payload, so the exactly-once guarantees recorded for the session decisions survive snapshot install and restart. The save path builds the snapshot metadata with the applied index and term, the membership, the request, the state machine type and compression type, plus a session buffer, and it fills that buffer by asking the session manager to save its sessions into it (statemachine.go:608-635). The session manager's save and load methods are thin wrappers over the LRU session table's own serialisation (sessionmanager.go:127-135), so the serialised form is the same table that the decision logic consults when a retried series arrives. The recovery path matches in the opposite direction and in the right order: the snapshotter opens the snapshot file, reads the header, wraps the stream in a decompressor, restores the sessions from that stream, and only then calls the user state machine's recover on the remaining stream before validating the payload (snapshotter.go:150-183). A node restored from a snapshot therefore still recognises a retried series as already applied rather than applying it twice. The one case that deliberately omits session state is the witness snapshot, which is written with an empty session table because a witness has no state machine and no client sessions (snapshotio.go:129-152); witness nodes reject proposals, reads, configuration changes and snapshot requests, so no client series can depend on session state there. Two bounds on the account: the trace covers the default snapshot path rather than each state machine variant, and it establishes that the sessions are written and read in the same order rather than exercising a real restore.

knowledge.assertion: The snapshot carries the session table and recovery restores it before the user payload, so session identity survives a snapshot.

counterevidence: The witness snapshot contains an empty session table, which is correct only because witness nodes cannot receive client proposals or session-managed entries; a non-witness node must never take that path.

The restore path validates the payload only after both the sessions and the payload have been consumed, so a corrupted snapshot can leave the session table populated in memory before the validation failure is detected.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the caller-side rule that makes the server's session deduplication effective is documented, consistent across both proposal entry points, and enforced by the session helper, so a proposal that times out is retried under the same series rather than being turned into a second command. The asynchronous entry point documents that when the result is a timeout the caller can retry the same proposal without updating the session, that a rejection usually means the server evicted the session and the client should be treated as failed, and that a successful completion requires calling ProposalCompleted to advance the session (nodehost.go:820-829). The synchronous entry point states the same rule in terms of its error values (nodehost.go:563-569), and the captured Chinese overview repeats it: after a successful proposal the application calls ProposalCompleted, while after a timeout it does not, and instead calls the proposal method again to retry (docs/overview.CHS.md:84). The session helper makes the discipline checkable rather than advisory: ProposalCompleted advances the series id and the acknowledged value only when the current series is exactly one ahead of the acknowledged value, panicking otherwise (client/session.go:104-120), and the pre-proposal validity check refuses a session whose acknowledged value has overtaken its series while reusing the same series is permitted (client/session.go:131-150). That is exactly the input the server needs: the recorded session decisions return the stored result without a state machine update when the same series is retried, which is why the contract can promise at-most-once application across a timeout. Two bounds belong with the account: the rule is a caller duty, so a client that advances the session on a timeout and then retries under a new series defeats deduplication by construction, and the documentation offers no mechanism to detect that misuse, since a new series is indistinguishable from a genuinely new command.

counterevidence: The contract is a caller duty: a client that calls ProposalCompleted after a timeout and then retries produces a new series, which the server cannot distinguish from a new command, so deduplication is defeated without any error being raised.

The rejection case is documented as usually meaning eviction, but the guidance is to treat the client as failed rather than to retry, so the safe path depends on the caller honouring a recommendation rather than on an enforced check.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a backlog of committed entries cannot be left half-applied by the bounded batching, because the update itself carries the signal that more work remains and the engine acts on it. The node side pushes the entries it was given as one task carrying those entries and records the last entry's index as the pushed index (node.go:582-588), so the batch boundary is explicit. The engine side reads the update's more-committed-entries flag after applying that batch and, when it is set, re-arms the cluster's step worker (engine.go:1348-1352), which is the same readiness mechanism the step loop uses to decide which clusters to visit next (engine.go:1290-1338). A cluster with a longer backlog is therefore revisited on the next iteration and the following batch is collected, rather than the remainder waiting for unrelated raft activity. Two bounds belong with the account: this is the engine's scheduling behaviour, so it says nothing about how quickly the state machine itself consumes a batch, and a state machine that blocks inside its own update routine holds the worker for that cluster regardless of the re-arm.

counterevidence: The re-arm depends on the update reporting that more committed entries remain; if that flag were not set while entries remained, the remainder would wait for other activity.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: a linearizable read cannot observe state older than the index the ReadIndex protocol confirmed, because the lookup is gated on the request state being completed by the applied-index pass rather than by the confirmation alone. The client side is explicit: SyncRead calls the linearizable-read helper with a closure that performs the state machine lookup, and the helper first resolves a read index, then waits for the returned request state, releases it, and only afterwards invokes the closure with the node (nodehost.go:597-611, 1485-1500). The read index step registers the request through the node and marks the cluster ready to step (nodehost.go:1468-1483), so the confirmation work is scheduled rather than performed inline. The gate itself is in the node layer: the applied-index pass completes a batch only when the batch carries a ready-to-read index and that index is at or below the node's applied index, and a batch whose index is still zero is skipped, which is why registration cannot complete a read on its own (request.go:908-937). Combined with the raft-side behaviour recorded earlier - the leader confirms a context only after quorum-1 matching heartbeat responses, and every state transition discards registered contexts - the answer a client receives reflects state applied up to a quorum-confirmed index, not merely the local applied index at the moment the request arrived. counterevidence: The gate bounds staleness, not freshness: entries applied after the confirmed index are visible to the lookup, so the returned state can be newer than the index that was confirmed.
Completion depends on the node's event loop continuing to run the applied-index pass; a node that stops applying holds the read until its deadline, which the earlier timeout account covers.

interpretations.rationale: Current claim: the missing membership check in the vote tally is not reachable as an election-safety problem, because a configuration change cannot take effect while the node is a candidate that holds votes. interpretations.rationale: Current claim for this question: a snapshot install leaves the node with one applied frontier, and the suspicion that committed entries could be replayed on top of recovered state or that later entries could be applied ahead of the recovery is refuted for the traced paths. Basis, in the order the node reaches it. (1) The raft layer adopts a snapshot only when its index is above the committed index, so the snapshot index is greater than every entry index the node has ever pushed to its state machine; a snapshot at or below committed is refused without being attached to any update, and when the log already holds the snapshot's index and term the log is not replaced and only the commit index moves. (2) An adopted snapshot is carried in every update from that peer until that update commits, and the update commit sets StableSnapshotTo to the snapshot index, raises Processed to at least that index and clears the in-memory snapshot pointer, so the same adopted snapshot is not redelivered by the peer. (3) In the engine, a snapshot update is marked not fast-appliable, is skipped by the first pass, and is processed only after the raft state write and the snapshot flag removal; processSnapshot records the snapshot in the log reader and pushSnapshot queues a Recover task, then applyRaftUpdates filters the same update's committed entries against the new pushed index. (4) entriesToApply drops every entry at or below pushedIndex, panics rather than silently skipping when the batch ends below it or starts beyond pushedIndex+1, and the union with (1) means an adopted snapshot can never present entries that are both above the frontier and separated from it by a hole. (5) Ordering is carried by the queue, not by a lock: the state machine applies entries queued before the recovery task, returns the recovery task to the apply loop when it reaches it, and refuses to handle anything queued behind it because the recovering flag makes processStatusTransition report the cluster as busy; the flag is cleared only after the recovery completion is read. (6) A recovery that finds the state machine already at or beyond the snapshot index is reported as an out-of-date snapshot and treated as an aborted recovery rather than an error, so even a recovery task that did reach the worker with a satisfied index ends without changing the frontier. The asymmetric part is deliberate and bounded: pushedIndex and the node's snapshot index move at queue time, while the state machine state moves at recovery completion, and the recovering gate is what covers that interval.
counterevidence: pushSnapshot sets pushedIndex and the node's snapshot index when the recovery task is queued, so for the duration of the asynchronous recovery the node's recorded frontier is ahead of the state machine's actual applied index; only the recovering flag and the queue order keep committed entries from being offered in that window.

Committed entries queued before the snapshot are applied to the state machine before the recovery task is handled and are then overwritten by the recovered snapshot state, so a snapshot install re-executes those updates rather than skipping them; this is idempotent only because the recovery replaces state at the snapshot index.

node.pushSnapshot treats a snapshot index equal to pushedIndex, to the node's snapshot index or to the applied index as acceptable and only panics when it is strictly lower, so the equal-index case relies on the raft layer's committed gate and on the state machine's out-of-date recovery result rather than on pushSnapshot's own comparison.
